name: Manzikert
summary: A walled town on the Murat plain north of Lake Van, fortified and fought over for centuries before the battle of 1071 made its name a turning point.
overview: A fortified town in eastern Anatolia, on the plain of the Murat north of Lake Van, remembered for the Byzantine defeat of 1071.
knownFor: The Byzantine defeat of August 1071 and the capture of Romanos IV Diogenes
Capital of the Kaysite emirate from about 860 until 964
Walls and a castle rebuilt under Seljuk rule in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Manzikert — Malazgirt in modern Turkish — stands on the open plain north of Lake Van, watered by the Murat, the eastern of the two great headwaters of the Euphrates. It sits in what Armenian geography called the canton of Apahunik in the province of Turuberan, and it was for centuries a fortified point on the frontier where Byzantine, Armenian, Arab and then Turkish power met.

That frontier position, not the town itself, explains its history. Manzikert was a place armies had to take because of where it lay, and it changed hands repeatedly. In August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes outside it and took him prisoner, and the town’s name became shorthand for the opening of Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

contentSections.title: The plain and the town
paragraphs: The setting is high, dry grassland with good water and long sight lines — country that suits horses and large armies, and that made this a natural corridor between the Iranian plateau, the Armenian highlands and the Anatolian interior. Settlement here is very old: the site is traced to the Iron Age and its foundation is associated with the Urartian king Menua, who reigned in the early eighth century BC.

For a medieval army the attraction was the combination of a fortified town with a plain around it broad enough to deploy on. That is precisely the shape of the 1071 campaign: Alp Arslan and Romanos IV were both operating for control of a fortress, and the battle was fought on the ground outside it.

contentSections.title: Before 1071: Kaysites, Byzantines and a repulsed siege
paragraphs: From about 860 until 964 Manzikert was the seat of the Kaysite emirate, an Arab frontier principality. In 968 the Byzantine general Bardas Phokas took the town, and by 1001 it had been annexed outright to the Byzantine Empire, part of the eastward expansion that also absorbed the Armenian principalities and put the empire’s border directly against the Turkish advance.

The Seljuks attempted the place before they succeeded: an attack in 1054 was beaten off by the garrison. Alp Arslan took it in the campaign of 1071 itself, shortly before the battle. The sequence matters, because it shows the town being contested for a generation before the year everyone remembers.

contentSections.title: The walls and the castle
paragraphs: Manzikert was a walled town, and its defences are the reason it appears in so many campaigns. After 1071 the fortifications were substantially rebuilt under Seljuk rule during the twelfth and, probably, the thirteenth centuries, and it is largely this Seljuk work — rather than anything Byzantine or Arab — that survives in the circuit and in Malazgirt Castle today.

The town paid for its position. After the battle the Seljuks sacked Manzikert itself, killed much of the population and burned it, so the walls a visitor sees stand over a settlement that had to be rebuilt after the very victory it is famous for.

contentSections.title: The town since the battle
paragraphs: Manzikert never became a great city. It is today a district town of some 42,000 people in Muş province, agricultural and provincial, and its fame rests entirely on a single August day nine and a half centuries ago. The battle is commemorated annually in the town, and the anniversary has become a fixed point of Turkish national commemoration.

For the archive the useful distinction is between the place and the event. The Battle of Manzikert was a political catastrophe for the Byzantine Empire, fought and lost on this plain; Manzikert the town was a fortress that changed hands, was burned, and was rebuilt by the winners.
